Let me analyze this OIML certificate carefully.

Certificate: R76/2006-GB1-17.14
- Issuing authority: NMO (UK)
- Person responsible: Mannie Panesar – Head of Technical Services
- Applicant: CAS Corporation, #262, Geurugogae-ro, Gwangjeok-myeon, Yangju-si, Gyeonggi-do, Republic of Korea
- Manufacturer: The applicant (CAS Corporation)
- Certified type: Dolphin Series (family of Class III weighing instruments), models EB, DBII, DB-1H
- Recommendation: OIML R76, Edition 2006(E), accuracy class III
- Issue date: 10 August 2017
- Evaluation Report P02162-2, 14 pages
- Scheme: This is an OIML-CS certificate. The scheme — R76/2006-GB1-17.14 — under the OIML-CS there are scheme A and B certificates. Certificates issued before MAA/CS... The format "R76/2006-GB1-17.14" is a national certificate format (GB1). The OIML-CS scheme A vs B — typically certificates issued under the MAA had "MAA" in number. This one is a national UK NMO certificate. Hmm, the schema says scheme (A|B). Since this predates/doesn't mention MAA or OIML-CS explicitly, but the certificate format follows OIML-CS layout ("OIML CERTIFICATE OF CONFORMITY", "Member State of OIML"). Under OIML-CS, national certificates under MAA were scheme... Actually in OIML-CS, Scheme A certificates are issued by Issuing Authorities of Member States without MAA participant review, and Scheme B are issued... Let me recall: OIML-CS Scheme A: certificates issued for Recommendations where the OIML-CS Committee has approved; single certificate from issuing authority. Scheme B: certificates issued where manufacturers... Actually:

OIML-CS (effective 2018) replaced MAA. Under OIML-CS:
- Scheme A: OIML certificate issued by an Issuing Authority, based on evaluation by an Issuing Authority of another Member State accepted... Hmm.

Actually: Scheme A — certificate issued based on test report done by Issuing Authority itself (nationally). Scheme B — certificate issued based on the recommendation... Let me think again. 

OIML-CS: There are two schemes:
- Scheme A: Issuing Authorities issue OIML certificates following evaluation by themselves (standard OIML certificates).
- Scheme B: applies to Recommendations where MAA was previously implemented — certificates issued based on evaluation reports validated...

Honestly, this level of detail may not be resolvable from the document. The document doesn't mention scheme A or B. The certificate number format "R76/2006-GB1-17.14" is a national scheme number. I could put scheme: null or "A". The schema says scheme (A|B). Given no info, I might omit scheme or set it null. Rule 8 says don't fabricate. I'll omit scheme or set null. Actually the layered schema shows scheme under certificate with (A|B) hint. Since it's not stated in the document, I'll omit it.

project_number: P02162-2 is the Evaluation Report number. That could be project_number: "P02162-2". The schema has project_number field. I'll use "P02162-2".

page_total: The evaluation report includes 14 pages. But "page_total" — certificate pages? The certificate shows "2 / 4", "3 / 4", "4 / 4" so 4 pages. Hmm, page_total could refer to the certificate's total pages = 4. The Evaluation Report has 14 pages, which goes into test_reports[].pages. I'll set page_total: 4.

date_issued: "10 August 2017" → "2017-08-10".

oiml_issuer_id: Not given explicitly. NMO... OIML issuing authority IDs... Not stated. Omit.

- name: NMO (National Measurement Office — the footer says "NMO is part of the Regulatory Delivery directorate..."). Name: "NMO".
- address_lines: ["Stanton Avenue", "Teddington", "TW11 0JZ", "United Kingdom"] — from "NMO I Stanton Avenue I Teddington I TW11 0JZ I United Kingdom".

Maybe keep G Stones out or... Rule: don't fabricate; the fields exist. I'll use Mannie Panesar as person responsible per the document.

applicants[]: name: "CAS Corporation", address_lines: ["#262, Geurugogae-ro", "Gwangjeok-myeon", "Yangju-si", "Gyeonggi-do", "Republic of Korea"]

manufacturers[]: "The applicant" → same as applicant: CAS Corporation with same address. Alternative manufacturers listed on page 4: CAS (Zhejiang) Electronics Co., Ltd (China), CAS Elektronik San. Tic. A.S. (Turkey), CAS Deutschland AG (Germany). These are alternative manufacturers — should they be in manufacturers[]? The header says "Manufacturer: The applicant", and page 4 lists "Alternative manufacturers". I'll include all: CAS Corporation plus the three alternatives. Each with name and address_lines.

certified_type:
- category: "Non-automatic weighing instrument" or "Weighing instrument". The category examples: "Load cell", "Indicator", "Measuring system", ... I'll use "Non-automatic weighing instrument".
- type_designations: ["Dolphin Series", "EB", "DBII", "DB-1H", "EB-L", "DB-1H PLUS", "DBII-C", "DBII-E"]. Hmm — type_designations: "all type/model identifiers mentioned". The certified pattern is "Dolphin Series". Models: EB, DBII, DB-1H; variants EB-L, DB-1H PLUS, DBII-C, DBII-E. I'll list: ["Dolphin Series", "EB", "DBII", "DB-1H", "EB-L", "DB-1H PLUS", "DBII-C", "DBII-E"].
- module_designation: These are complete instruments, not modules. The One-Module V4 is the software/indicator module? "using the One-Module V4" — that refers to the instrument being a single module indicator? Actually "One-Module V4" is software identification version. For a complete weighing instrument, module_designation: "Not applicable". Hmm — but the instrument "uses the One-Module V4" software. I'd say module_designation: "Not applicable" since it's a complete instrument. Or null. I'll put "Not applicable".
- description: "The Dolphin Series is a family of Class III, mains or battery-operated, self-indicating, dual-interval, non-automatic weighing instruments. It comprises the EB, DBII and DB-1H models and their variants (Figures 1 to 4), using the One-Module V4. The instrument may be used for direct sales to the public."

model_family:
- family_name: "Dolphin Series"
- models: variants. The models: EB, EB-L, DBII-C (LCD), DBII-E (LED), DB-1H PLUS. And load cell options BCO/BCA. Let me enumerate from the "Model variants and designation" table:
  - EB, BCO, LCD, variant "EB", option RS232
  - EB, BCO, LCD, variant "EB-L", option RS232, remark "Larger weighing platform"
  - DB-1H, BCO, VFD, variant "DB-1H PLUS", option RS232, remarks "Printing mode; Weighing unstable samples mode"
  - DBII, BCO, LCD, variant "DBII-C", option RS232
  - DBII, BCO, LED, variant "DBII-E", option RS232
  - DBII, BCA, LCD, variant "DBII-C", option RS232
  - DBII, BCA, LED, variant "DBII-E", option RS232

So models with attributes. model_id could be the variant designation: "EB", "EB-L", "DB-1H PLUS", "DBII-C", "DBII-E". With attributes: display, load_cell, option.

But capacity variants also exist: The metrological characteristics tables give:
Table 1: Model EB/DBII/DB-1H with BCO Load Cell:
- Max (kg): "30/60 kg" and "60/150 kg" — two capacity variants. Dual interval instruments: Max = 30/60 kg means Max1=30, Max2=60? For dual-interval instruments, "Max" listed as "30/60" likely means maximum capacity for each of the two intervals... Actually for dual-interval, typically Min₁/Max₁ and Min₂/Max₂. The table:
  - Max (kg): 30/60 kg | 60/150 kg
  - Min (g): 200 g | 400 g
  - e (g): 10/20 g | 20/50 g
  - T ≤ (kg): -29.99 kg | -59.98 kg

Hmm, T ≤ (kg): "-29.99 kg" — that looks odd; tare is typically negative up to... Actually initial tare? "T ≤ -29.99 kg" is weird. It might be the subtractive tare range: up to 29.99 kg (i.e., -29.99). So T ≤ -29.99 kg meaning tare can go down to -29.99 kg. This is likely Max₁ - e = 30 - 0.01 = 29.99. So subtractive tare range equals Max₁ minus one interval.

For the dual-interval interpretation: Max 30/60 means for the two intervals: interval 1 up to 30 kg with e=10g? Wait e: 10/20 g — so e₁=10 g, e₂=20 g. And Max 30/60: Max₁ = 30 kg, Max₂ = 60 kg. Hmm but Min 200 g — for dual interval, Min₁ = 20e₁ = 200g. Yes! Min = 20e₁ = 20×10 = 200 g. And second column: e₁=20, e₂=50; Min = 400 g = 20×20. Max₁=60, Max₂=150. T ≤ -29.99 kg: Max₁ - e₁ = 60 - 0.02 = 59.98 ✓. First column: 30 - 0.01 = 29.99 ✓. So this confirms the dual-interval reading: Max₁/Max₂, e₁/e₂, T ≤ -(Max₁ - e₁).

Table 2: DBII with BCA Load Cell:
- Max (kg): 3/6, 6/15, 15/30 (three capacity variants)
- Min (g): 20, 40, 100
- e (g): 1/2, 2/5, 5/10
- T ≤ (kg): -2.999, -5.998, -14.995

Check: Max₁=3, e₁=1g → 3-0.001=2.999 ✓. Max₁=6, e₁=2g → 6-0.002=5.998 ✓. Max₁=15, e₁=5g → 15-0.005=14.995 ✓.

So capacity variants:
BCO models (EB/DBII/DB-1H): capacity groups A: Max 30/60, e 10/20, Min 200g; group B: Max 60/150, e 20/50, Min 400g.
BCA DBII: groups: 3/6 (e 1/2, min 20g), 6/15 (e 2/5, min 40g), 15/30 (e 5/10, min 100g).

This is complex: two dimensions — model variant (EB, EB-L, DB-1H PLUS, DBII-C, DBII-E) × capacity group. The table 1 says "EB / DBII / DB-1H with BCO Load Cell" — so both capacity groups apply to EB, DBII, DB-1H with BCO. Table 2 says DBII with BCA only.

How to model this? Options:
1. model_level matrix with attributes max, min, verification_scale_interval, tare_limit, with model IDs combining variant+capacity, e.g., "EB 30/60 kg", "EB 60/150 kg", etc.
2. matrix_tables preserving the two tables.

Given the instruction "preserve multi-dim tables that don't fit elsewhere" in matrix_tables and "attribute × model matrix" in model_level — I think I should do both: define models as variant × capacity combos, and emit model_level entries for max, min, e, T.

But that could explode: variants EB, EB-L, DB-1H PLUS (BCO) × 2 capacities + DBII-C, DBII-E × BCO × 2 capacities + DBII-C, DBII-E × BCA × 3 capacities = 2×2 + 2×2 + 2×3 = 4+4+6 = 14 combos. That's a lot but manageable. However, the certificate itself groups them as "EB / DBII / DB-1H with BCO" for capacities and "DBII with BCA". Maybe simpler: treat models as the variant designations (EB, EB-L, DB-1H PLUS, DBII-C, DBII-E) and use matrix_tables to preserve the capacity tables, plus config_level or model_level at the capacity-group level.

Hmm. Let me think about the cleanest representation that follows the schema spirit:

- model_family.models: one entry per variant: EB, EB-L, DB-1H PLUS, DBII-C (BCO), DBII-E (BCO), DBII-C (BCA), DBII-E (BCA). Model IDs: "EB", "EB-L", "DB-1H PLUS", "DBII-C", "DBII-E". Since DBII-C appears with both BCO and BCA load cells, maybe model_id should include load cell: "DBII-C (BCO)", "DBII-E (BCO)", "DBII-C (BCA)", "DBII-E (BCA)".

- For the capacity variants, since the certificate presents them per load-cell table rather than per model designation, I could use config_level with axis "capacity_group" or matrix_tables.

Given rule 5 says configuration axes for attributes varying by configuration. The capacity variation is a real model variation though. But the certificate treats capacities as shared across models with the same load cell.

I think the most faithful approach:
- matrix_tables: two tables "Metrological characteristics — EB/DBII/DB-1H with BCO load cell" and "Metrological characteristics — DBII with BCA load cell", preserving columns.
- model_level characteristics: attributes max, min, e, tare_limit with values per capacity-group model like "BCO 30/60 kg", "BCO 60/150 kg", "BCA 3/6 kg", "BCA 6/15 kg", "BCA 15/30 kg". Hmm but that conflates.

Alternatively, model_level with model IDs like "EB/DBII/DB-1H with BCO, Max 30/60 kg"... getting messy.

Let me choose a pragmatic design:

model_family.models: entries for each variant designation × load cell × capacity group:
- model_id: "EB-30/60" ... too invented.

Alternative: keep models as the 5 named variants (EB, EB-L, DB-1H PLUS, DBII-C, DBII-E), with attributes {display, load_cell_options, options}. Then use config_level for capacity groups? Rule 5's example: "2-sensor-row vs 4-sensor-row setups". Capacity group is more like a model attribute.

Actually, let me reconsider: the certificate's metrological tables key off load cell (BCO vs BCA), not off variant name. The capacity groups:

BCO (EB, DBII, DB-1H):
- Group 1: Max1=30 kg, Max2=60 kg, Min=200 g, e1=10 g, e2=20 g, T≤29.99 kg
- Group 2: Max1=60 kg, Max2=150 kg, Min=400 g, e1=20 g, e2=50 g, T≤59.98 kg

BCA (DBII only):
- Group 1: Max 3/6 kg, Min 20 g, e 1/2 g, T≤2.999 kg
- Group 2: Max 6/15 kg, Min 40 g, e 2/5 g, T≤5.998 kg
- Group 3: Max 15/30 kg, Min 100 g, e 5/10 g, T≤14.995 kg

I'll create models combining variant and capacity:

For model_level characteristics, I'll use model IDs like "EB (BCO, Max 30/60 kg)", "EB (BCO, Max 60/150 kg)", "DBII-C (BCO, Max 30/60 kg)", ... That's 14 model IDs. Then attributes: maximum_capacity_interval_1 (max1), maximum_capacity_interval_2 (max2), minimum_capacity, scale_interval_e1, scale_interval_e2, tare_limit.

Hmm, this is heavy but accurate. Alternatively simpler: use the capacity group as the model axis:

model_level entries with model IDs: "BCO 30/60 kg", "BCO 60/150 kg", "BCA 3/6 kg", "BCA 6/15 kg", "BCA 15/30 kg".

And matrix_tables preserving the original tables.

I think I'll go with a middle ground: model_family.models lists the seven variant+loadcell combos (EB, EB-L, DB-1H PLUS, DBII-C BCO, DBII-E BCO, DBII-C BCA, DBII-E BCA) with attributes for display, option, remarks, and capacity_groups available. Then matrix_tables preserves the two capacity tables verbatim. And model_level... hmm, model_level is "attribute × model matrix". If models are the 7 combos, then max/min/e vary within a model (per capacity group) — that violates single-value-per-model.

Given the ambiguity, I'll define models as capacity-group-specific combos. Let me enumerate 14:

BCO capacity groups apply to EB, DBII, DB-1H:
1. EB | BCO | 30/60 → "EB 30/60 kg"
2. EB | BCO | 60/150 → "EB 60/150 kg"
3. EB-L | BCO | 30/60 → "EB-L 30/60 kg"
4. EB-L | BCO | 60/150 → "EB-L 60/150 kg"
5. DB-1H PLUS | BCO | 30/60 → "DB-1H PLUS 30/60 kg"
6. DB-1H PLUS | BCO | 60/150 → "DB-1H PLUS 60/150 kg"
7. DBII-C | BCO | 30/60 → "DBII-C (BCO) 30/60 kg"
8. DBII-E | BCO | 30/60
9. DBII-C (BCO) 60/150
10. DBII-E (BCO) 60/150
11. DBII-C (BCA) 3/6
12. DBII-E (BCA) 3/6
13. DBII-C (BCA) 6/15
14. DBII-E (BCA) 6/15
15. DBII-C (BCA) 15/30
16. DBII-E (BCA) 15/30

That's 16. Hmm wait: EB/DBII/DB-1H with BCO = EB, EB-L, DB-1H PLUS, DBII-C, DBII-E = 5 variants × 2 = 10; DBII-C/E with BCA = 2 × 3 = 6; total 16. That's a lot of model entries but it is accurate.

That seems overly exploded and risks fabrication (assuming EB-L comes in both capacity groups — the table says "EB / DBII / DB-1H with BCO Load Cell" covers both capacity columns, and EB-L is an EB variant with larger platform, so presumably yes, but the cert doesn't explicitly say EB-L is in the metrological table).

Given "Don't fabricate", maybe safer to keep models at the level the certificate states: the metrological tables are per load cell group, not per variant. So:

- model_family.models: 
  - {"model_id": "EB", "attributes": {"load_cell": "BCO", "display": "LCD", "option": "RS232"}}
  - {"model_id": "EB-L", "attributes": {"load_cell": "BCO", "display": "LCD", "option": "RS232", "remarks": "Larger weighing platform"}}
  - {"model_id": "DB-1H PLUS", "attributes": {"load_cell": "BCO", "display": "VFD", "option": "RS232", "remarks": "Printing mode; Weighing unstable samples mode"}}
  - {"model_id": "DBII-C (BCO)", "attributes": {"load_cell": "BCO", "display": "LCD", "option": "RS232"}}
  - {"model_id": "DBII-E (BCO)", ...LED}
  - {"model_id": "DBII-C (BCA)", ...}
  - {"model_id": "DBII-E (BCA)", ...}

- characteristics.model_level: attributes keyed by capacity group. Since certificate groups capacities by load cell table, I'll create model_level entries with model IDs "EB/DBII/DB-1H (BCO) 30/60 kg" style? That invents composite IDs.

Alternatively use config_level with axis "capacity_group":

config_level:
- attribute: "maximum_capacity", axis: "load_cell_and_capacity_group", values: [{condition: "BCO, capacity group 1", value: {min:30, max:60}...}] — wait, Max 30/60 for dual interval is two Max values (Max1 and Max2), not a range! Important: Max "30/60 kg" is NOT a range 30–60; it's Max1=30, Max2=60 (two intervals). Similarly e "10/20 g" is e1=10, e2=20.

So I should represent as separate attributes:
- max_capacity_interval_1: 30 kg
- max_capacity_interval_2: 60 kg
- e_interval_1: 10 g
- e_interval_2: 20 g
- minimum_capacity: 200 g
- tare_limit: 29.99 kg (value negative in cert: "T ≤ -29.99 kg" — the minus sign indicates subtractive tare; the value is -29.99 kg with condition ≤).

Hmm, the cert literally writes "T ≤ (kg): -29.99 kg". So tare ≤ -29.99? That reads oddly but means the subtractive tare goes down to -29.99 kg, i.e., tare up to 29.99 kg. I'll record as attribute "tare_limit" with value -29.99 kg as written, or value 29.99 with note. To avoid misinterpretation, record value: -29.99, unit kg, attribute "maximum_subtractive_tare" maybe. Hmm. The safest is attribute "tare_limit" value -29.99 kg (as printed). I'll use canonical label "tare_limit" with the negative value as printed. Actually "T ≤ -29.99" means T is at most -29.99 kg... In OIML R76 notation, subtractive tare is negative. I'll keep value -29.99.

OK here's my decision on structure for metrological data:

matrix_tables: preserve both tables with rows per capacity variant:

Table 1: name "Metrological characteristics — EB / DBII / DB-1H with BCO load cell"
columns: ["max_interval_1_kg", "max_interval_2_kg", "min_g", "e_interval_1_g", "e_interval_2_g", "tare_limit_kg"]? The original table has rows as attributes and columns as capacity variants. Schema: columns[], rows[] (object per row). So transpose: each row = one capacity variant.

columns: ["capacity_group", "max_1", "max_2", "min", "e_1", "e_2", "tare_limit"]
column_units: [null, "kg", "kg", "g", "g", "g", "kg"]
rows:
- {"capacity_group": "1", "max_1": 30, "max_2": 60, "min": 200, "e_1": 10, "e_2": 20, "tare_limit": -29.99}
- {"capacity_group": "2", "max_1": 60, "max_2": 150, "min": 400, "e_1": 20, "e_2": 50, "tare_limit": -59.98}

Table 2: "Metrological characteristics — DBII with BCA load cell"
rows:
- {"capacity_group": "1", "max_1": 3, "max_2": 6, "min": 20, "e_1": 1, "e_2": 2, "tare_limit": -2.999}
- {"capacity_group": "2", "max_1": 6, "max_2": 15, "min": 40, "e_1": 2, "e_2": 5, "tare_limit": -5.998}
- {"capacity_group": "3", "max_1": 15, "max_2": 30, "min": 100, "e_1": 5, "e_2": 10, "tare_limit": -14.995}

Also the "Model variants and designation" table → matrix_tables third entry? It's captured in model_family.models attributes, so maybe not needed as matrix table. I'll capture it in model_family.

characteristics.model_level: Hmm. Given models are variant designations, and capacities vary per load-cell group... I could add model_level entries for max/min/e keyed by a "model" string that encodes load cell + capacity group, e.g. "BCO group 1 (30/60 kg)". But rule 4 example ties model IDs to model_family.models. To be consistent, I could set model_family.models to include capacity variants after all.

Let me reconsider: Perhaps cleaner to define model_family.models with capacity-inclusive IDs, matching how such extractions typically work, and accept 16 entries. Actually wait — is it certain EB-L and DB-1H PLUS come in both capacity groups? The table 1 header: "Model: EB / DBII / DB-1H with BCO Load Cell" with columns 30/60 and 60/150. So EB, DBII, DB-1H each in both capacity groups. EB-L is an EB variant (larger platform) — presumably same capacities but not explicitly stated. To avoid fabricating, better NOT to explode variants × capacities.

Final decision: keep models as the 7 variant+loadcell combos; put metrological capacity data in matrix_tables AND in model_level keyed by load-cell+capacity-group composite IDs like "EB/DBII/DB-1H (BCO) — 30/60 kg"? That mixes.

Alternatively, use config_level for capacities with axis "load cell and capacity variant". Rule 5: configuration axes when attributes vary by configuration. Capacity group is arguably a configuration dimension shared across models. I'll use config_level:

config_level:
- {attribute: "maximum_capacity_interval_1", axis: "load cell / capacity group", values: [
    {condition: "BCO, capacity group 1", value: 30, unit_symbol: "kg"},
    {condition: "BCO, capacity group 2", value: 60, unit_symbol: "kg"},
    {condition: "BCA, capacity group 1 (DBII only)", value: 3, unit_symbol: "kg"},
    {condition: "BCA, capacity group 2 (DBII only)", value: 6, unit_symbol: "kg"},
    {condition: "BCA, capacity group 3 (DBII only)", value: 15, unit_symbol: "kg"}
  ]}
- maximum_capacity_interval_2 similarly: 60, 150, 6, 15, 30
- minimum_capacity: 200 g, 400 g, 20 g, 40 g, 100 g
- verification_scale_interval_e_1: 10, 20, 1, 2, 5 g
- verification_scale_interval_e_2: 20, 50, 2, 5, 10 g
- tare_limit: -29.99, -59.98, -2.999, -5.998, -14.995 kg

That's reasonably faithful. Plus matrix_tables preserving the original tables. Good.

Hmm, but "condition" strings like "BCO, capacity group 1" — the cert labels columns just "30/60 kg" and "60/150 kg". I'll use conditions: "BCO load cell, Max 30/60 kg", "BCO load cell, Max 60/150 kg", "BCA load cell, Max 3/6 kg (DBII only)", etc. That embeds the value in the condition, slightly redundant but clear.

type_level characteristics:
- accuracy_class: "III" — well that's in recommendation. Could add class: {value: "III"}.
- temperature_range: {min: -10, max: 40}, unit °C. "The temperature range for the instruments is -10 °C / +40 °C."
- software identification: "V4.xx.x" — attribute software_version or software_identification: {value: "V4.xx.x"}. Note: "The software identification shall be V4.xx.x, with xx.x reflecting non-legally relevant changes."
- initial_zero_setting_device_range: ≤ 20% of Max → attribute "initial_zero_setting_range", value {max: 20}, unit "%", and maybe reference Max. I'll do value {min: null, max: 20}, unit_symbol "%", and maybe a separate note. Keep simple: attribute initial_zero_setting_range.
- automatic_zero_setting_range: ≤ 4% of Max
- zero_tracking_range: ≤ 4% of Max
- power supply: from technical data table: EB 12 VDC, DBII 12 VDC, DB-1H 230VAC; footnote * "The instruments operate directly on a 230 V AC supply or via a remote power adaptor (12 V DC), or directly on the integrated battery or set of batteries."

Technical data table is a model×attribute matrix:

Capacities: All, All, All
Display: LCD, LCD/LED, VFD
Voltage: 12 VDC *, 12 VDC *, 230VAC

This is a model_level matrix with models EB, DBII, DB-1H:
- display: EB=LCD, DBII=LCD/LED, DB-1H=VFD
- supply_voltage: EB=12 VDC, DBII=12 VDC, DB-1H=230 VAC
- battery: EB="Integrated rechargeable 6V 3.6Ah", DBII=same, DB-1H="No"

But wait — this conflicts with my model_family model IDs (EB, EB-L, DB-1H PLUS, DBII-C/E). The display per model: DBII-C is LCD, DBII-E is LED — consistent with "LCD/LED". Display battery values are strings, not numbers — that's fine, values can be strings.

For model_level entries, which model ID set to use? The technical data table uses EB, DBII, DB-1H. The variant table uses EB, EB-L, DB-1H PLUS, DBII-C, DBII-E. I think model IDs in model_level should match model_family.models. Let me define model_family.models as the 7 combos (or 5 combos — DBII-C/E have both BCO and BCA rows in variant table).

Variant table rows:
- EB | BCO | LCD | EB | RS232
- EB | BCO | LCD | EB-L | RS232 | Larger weighing platform
- DB-1H | BCO | VFD | DB-1H PLUS | RS232 | Printing mode; Weighing unstable samples mode
- DBII | BCO | LCD | DBII-C | RS232
- DBII | BCO | LED | DBII-E | RS232
- DBII | BCA | LCD | DBII-C | RS232
- DBII | BCA | LED | DBII-E | RS232

So variant designations: EB, EB-L, DB-1H PLUS, DBII-C, DBII-E. DBII-C and DBII-E each available with BCO or BCA.

model_family.models — I'll use 5 entries keyed by variant designation, with attributes:
